stories.headline: It is the responsibility of top athletes to look after the sports administration: Nehwal
stories.deck: The shuttler, who has won the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) election of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) polls, saids she feels the need to give it back to the sport.
stories.bodyText:
Pune: London Olympics bronze medallistshuttler 
Saina Nehwal
 feels involvement of former top athletes in the administrative roles can lift the standard of Indian sports.
The shuttler, who has won the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) election of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) polls, saids she feels the need to give it back to the sport. “It is a very good sign that sports is now being looked after by people who have played at the highest level. A lot of knowledge can be shared among these sportspersons, who come from different disciplines. Whatever knowledge I have gained from badminton, I will be able to share with theathletes, and similarly, I can learn from their experiences. We can collectively discuss what is required to build more champions and strengthen the sporting system in India,” she told TOI.
“We have the Commonwealth Games coming up, and we are also looking at hosting the Olympics. Having experienced sportspersons in sports administration will only help improve our results and medal tally,” she said.
Saina has won an Olympic medal and has recently retired from active badminton. She feels staying in touch with the sport makes it better for the administrators to understand the need of the sport better.
“As you grow older, you begin to understand what it takes to make a champion and what all is required to achieve that. 
When I look at countries such as China and Korea, I notice that their sports associations are often headed by people who have themselves performed at the highest level and won Olympic medals. I strongly believe that experienced sportspersons who have performed at the highest level should be involved in every aspect of sports administration.
 They understand what is happening on the ground and what athletes actually need. They travel extensively with players and understand the challenges they face.”
On the possibility of her contesting for the post of the president, she said, “I don't know. Whether it is me or any other sportsperson, it hardly matters. What matters is that we work together to improve Indian sport and increase our medal tally. We should aim to reach the level of countries such as China and America.The position of president or any other post will obviously have a name associated with it. But ultimately, the important thing is how we work together and what we can collectively achieve to win more medals for the country.”

briefs.headline: Sonia Gandhi memoir: 1966 fight between Ali and Cooper that former Cong prez remembers
briefs.deck: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's memoir recalls the Wembley bout of 1966
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Sonia and the '60s is also a tale of a young girl swept in the tide of civil rights blowing across the globe.
In her memoir 'Belonging', mentioning Martin Luther King, "free speech movement" in Berkeley and students movements in Europe as the influences on her generation, the Congress matriarch has fleetingly, but noticeably, referred to an indelible episode from the timeless story of boxing great 
Muhammad Ali
. This was among the "memorable moments" in Cambridge after Sonia met Rajiv Gandhi. On a May 1966 evening, Sonia and friends gathered at a friend's place glued to the radio to listen to "the blow-by-blow boxing match between Ali and British boxer Henry Cooper."
She adds, "when Clay beat Cooper in the sixth round of the match, we roared in triumph. It was for us not just a victory in a sport but a moral one as well. We had been roused by Martin Luther King Jr's massive demonstration in Washington and his 'I have a dream' speech."
It was a momentous evening - not just for the prize fight - but for the times it represented. Two years ago, Ali had not only become the world heavyweight champion, acquired a reputation as a blabbermouth, but also a flaming rebel and a political lightening rod who shook the white establishment of Jim Crow America with his black pride assertion.
A rebellion that would take him to oppose the draft to fight in the Vietnam War with that stinging barb - "I ain't got no quarrel with 'em VietCong". 
It led to his exile from boxing, before his return four years later shook the world more than his initial avatar, interspersed with gladiatorial battles like 'Rumble in the Jungle' and 'Thrilla in Manila'. But prior to Ali's exile were his two fights with Cooper, the British champion. The first was in 1963 as Cassius Clay, then still a braggard who backed his claims with heavy punches and floored opponents with blinding speed. Clay went to London in the hope of mopping up points to force the reigning heavyweight champion, the scary Sonny Liston to give him a chance at the title.
This was the fight that is remembered for trainer Angelo Dundee's gamesmanship that saved the day for Clay and kept him in business for future. Who knows if it had turned out differently.
Clay had mocked Cooper like he did to all - predicting to end it in five rounds. But 'Enry's 'Ammer', that dreaded left hook (hammer) that Cooper was famous for, put Clay on his backside in the fourth round. Ali later said, "it made me feel as if I had gone back and visited all my ancestors in Africa". It was enough, almost. But a small split in the seam of one glove, that trainer Angelo Dundee had seen before the fight but retained presciently for an emergency, was now put to good use .
As Ali "slumped on his stool like a sack of potatoes", Dundee stuck his finger in the split and made it bigger and then asked the referee for a change of gloves. That earned Clay enough seconds to return to his senses. He recovered to batter Cooper. A year later, Clay shocked the world by defeating Liston twice, embraced Islam and became the most famous man on earth.

The 31-year-old has been included in the squad for the fourth and fifth ODIs against India. He is also in line to make his international debut in the fourth match, which will be played on Friday.
India lead the five-match series 2-0 after winning the first two games. The third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned due to rain.
Randell has played 145 professional matches, including five for New Zealand A. He recently returned from a stint with English county side Derbyshire in the County Championship.
New Zealand Cricket has also added all-rounder 
Josh Clarkson
 to the squad for the fifth and final ODI, scheduled for Sunday.
Randell's record-breaking five wickets in five balls
Randell created history while playing for Central Stags against Northern Districts in New Zealand's Plunket Shield in March this year. The 31-year-old took five wickets in five consecutive balls on the second day of the match, becoming the first bowler in the 254-year history of first-class cricket to achieve the feat.
While Randell was the first to do it in first-class cricket, five wickets in five balls had been achieved in other formats before.
Ireland's Curtis Campher became the first male player to take five wickets in five balls in a professional match during a domestic T20 game in July 2025.
Zimbabwe Women all-rounder Kelis Ndhlovu had also achieved the feat in a domestic Under-19 T20 match in 2024.
New Zealand coach backs Randell
New Zealand head coach Rob Walter congratulated Randell on his first international call-up and praised his consistent performances in domestic cricket.
"It's always a special time when a player earns their first international call up," said Walter.
"We're very pleased for Brett, he's been a consistent performer in domestic cricket for some time now and has earned this opportunity. There’s been a few movements throughout the series so we're fortunate to be able to bring in Brett and Josh," he said.
Changes to New Zealand coaching staff
New Zealand Cricket has also made changes to its coaching staff as the team starts preparing for the Test series against India, which begins on November 19.
Northern Districts pathway coach Mitch Renwick and strength and conditioning coach Corey Mileys have joined head coach Walter and Martin Guptill for the ODI series.
Regular bowling coach Jacob Oram, batting coach Luke Ronchi and strength and conditioning coach Chris Donaldson have left the ODI squad and moved to Wellington to prepare for the Test series.
New Zealand's updated ODI squads
Fourth ODI: Mitchell Santner (C), Finn Allen, Michael Bracewell, Kristian Clarke, Jacob Duffy, Matt Fisher, Dean Foxcroft, Mitch Hay (WK), Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Nick Kelly, Brett Randell, Tim Seifert (WK), Will Young.
Fifth ODI: Mitchell Santner (C), Finn Allen, Michael Bracewell, Kristian Clarke, Josh Clarkson, Jacob Duffy, Matt Fisher, Dean Foxcroft, Mitch Hay (WK), Nick Kelly, Brett Randell, Tim Seifert (WK), Blair Tickner, Will Young.

briefs.headline: Axar Patel reluctant to lead, Delhi Capitals in a fix ahead of IPL auction
briefs.deck: TOI has learnt that incumbent captain Axar Patel has expressed his reluctance to lead the team after going through two tough seasons.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: As the IPL franchises begin planning for next month's mini auction, Delhi Capitals are in a fix over identifying their captain for the next season. TOI has learnt that incumbent captain 
Axar Patel
 has expressed his reluctance to lead the team after going through two tough seasons.
Sources said that the franchise doesn't want to rule out Axar as captain, but it may take a lot of effort to convince him to continue with the job. Capitals failed to qualify for the playoffs in the last two seasons. While they came close in 2025, the last season wasn't a pleasant one as they finished sixth. Axar suffered a dip in form last year, scoring just 173 runs and taking 11 wickets in 14 matches.
"Axar is very reluctant to continue as captain. The management is trying to convince him. Axar is very important to the franchise. Capitals have turned down multiple lucrative trade offers this season. The management has held back finalising the captain till the auctions are done," a source told TOI.
Capitals have carried out an overhaul of the coaching staff by bringing Sourav Ganguly back in the fold as the head coach and 
Yuvraj Singh
 as the assistant coach after the franchise parted ways with previous head coach Hemang Badani and director of cricket Venugopal Rao. There are suggestions that the team's leadership group struggled to be on the same page as Badani and Rao which has led to Axar's indecision.

briefs.headline: 'Mumbai were keen on Arshdeep': Ness Wadia reveals how Hardik trade materialised
briefs.deck: Punjab Kings co-owner Ness Wadia opens up about the blockbuster Hardik Pandya-Arshdeep Singh trade, admitting that letting go of the India pacer was a difficult decision. Wadia explains the cricketing rationale behind acquiring Pandya, reveals how the negotiations unfolded and outlines the franchise's long-term ambitions of building a championship-winning team.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Punjab Kings co-owner Ness Wadia, a lifelong Arsenal fan, believes 
Hardik Pandya
 could bring the midas touch that the Mohali-based franchise has been missing over the last couple of seasons. Despite showing plenty of promise over the past two seasons, Punjab Kings have fallen short of winning their maiden Indian Premier League (
IPL
) title. Wadia feels the India all-rounder could be the missing piece in the Shreyas Iyer-led side's puzzle and help the franchise dominate the league, much like his favourite club Arsenal are doing in the Premier League.
In a freewheeling chat with TimesofIndia.com, Punjab Kings co-owner Ness Wadia opens up about the blockbuster Hardik Pandya-Arshdeep Singh trade, admitting that letting go of the India pacer was a difficult decision. Wadia explains the cricketing rationale behind acquiring Pandya, reveals how the negotiations unfolded and outlines the franchise's long-term ambitions of building a championship-winning team.
Excerpts
How long did it take for the Hardik Pandya-Arshdeep Singh trade to materialise?
Ness Wadia:
 Yes, it took a little while. I think 
Mumbai Indians
 were keen on Arshdeep, and from a cricketing perspective, we also reflected on it a lot. We believe Hardik is someone who brings a great deal to the team. Most importantly, this is not about a short-term, one-year arrangement. We are keen to build a very strong franchise that wins championships, and we feel this move will take us in that direction. We are looking at Hardik as a long-term investment, not just a short-term move.
Was it always going to be a straight swap, or were other players also discussed?
Ness Wadia:
 It was always going to be a direct swap.
Punjab Kings' Arshdeep Singh joins Mumbai Indians in much-anticipated IPL player trade.
Arshdeep is someone Punjab Kings have invested in from a young age. He is also a local boy from Mohali and has become one of the faces of the franchise. How difficult was it to let him go?
Ness Wadia:
 There are two ways to look at it. The way I see it, it makes me happy that he has done so well. It makes me happy that he is so much in demand. At the end of the day, it makes me exceedingly happy that he represents our country at the highest level and is one of its leaders. So, there is only happiness. That is what I have to say.
What kind of conversation did you have with Hardik Pandya?
Ness Wadia:
 We had a very good conversation with Hardik. I think he will bring a lot of experience and add tremendous value to Shreyas and Ricky. He worked with Ricky during his initial years at Mumbai Indians and has a lot of respect for him. I think this will be a win-win situation for everyone.
In the past couple of seasons, Punjab Kings have been doing well, much like the Gunners, before they went on to win the Premier League. I think we are almost there. Hardik brings that Midas touch to us.
Hardik Pandya moves to Punjab Kings from Mumbai Indians in much-anticipated IPL player trade.
Punjab Kings were already a strong and consistent team, but Hardik's arrival seems to add something that could help the side go all the way. Was Hardik the missing piece over the last couple of seasons?
Ness Wadia:
 No puzzle is ever perfectly complete. All the players have to come together and perform well. Timing is very important, and players go through ups and downs. But I think, as a collective group under the leadership of Shreyas and Ricky, we have proved that we can stand up and deliver.
We reached the final in 2025, and were doing really well in 2026, before slipping up towards the end. I think that was down to a lack of experience. Sometimes, overconfidence also creeps in. There were also players who did not perform at their expected levels. But we certainly have the potential to win not just one, but several championships. That is the objective for Hardik, Shreyas, Ricky and all of us.
You have been part of the IPL as an owner since its inception and have seen the league grow over the years. How much has the business evolved? With the introduction of the trading window, do you see the possibility of a mid-season transfer window in the future?
Ness Wadia:
 The league has to keep evolving. I think it is good that the trading window was introduced and that it remains open even after the retention deadline. It is interesting because a lot of trades have happened this year.
It shows that franchises are willing to make difficult calls, go into an auction, do the best they can and then assess how things work out over the next one or two years. They can subsequently make adjustments and tweak their squads. But as far as we are concerned, we are looking at Hardik as a long-term investment, not just a short-term move.
Ness Wadia (Image Credits: Ness Wadia Instagram)
Are there any more trades in store for Punjab Kings, or will we next see the franchise in action at the auction in Goa?
Ness Wadia: You never know. Stranger things have happened! We still have few days left, so a lot can happen in that time. These things can move very quickly.
Of course, if a trade is on the cards, franchises can always agree and complete it even after the retention deadline. That is the beauty of having the trading window open after retentions as well.
There have been discussions and reports about extending the IPL window. What is your take on that? Do you see merit in having a longer window or shifting the tournament to a different period?
Ness Wadia:
 As far as the IPL window is concerned, it would be good to have a different window because, with changing weather patterns, it sometimes starts raining or gets very hot, making conditions difficult for players. Ideally, one could look at shifting the tournament.
However, we will have to consider the domestic and international cricket calendars and see what is possible. But it is certainly something worth exploring.
How difficult is it for a franchise to play its home matches across two different venues?
Ness Wadia:  It is difficult. It is difficult for the players as well. But we have to look at the bigger picture. At the end of the day, it is also about the revenue we generate and the support we receive from both the PC and HPC. It would be fantastic if that support continues.
Let's see how things develop going forward. Having said that, these are world-class players, and everyone adjusts and adapts. You can look at it as having one additional venue.
But doesn't splitting home matches between two venues take away the home advantage? For franchises like MI and CSK , one of the secrets of their success has been playing seven home games at the same venue. Punjab Kings, on the other hand, have to divide their matches between Mohali and Dharamsala.
Ness Wadia: It is a valid point, and I understand that perspective.

briefs.headline: Youth Olympics: Gunjan one win away from gold after reaching 48kg final
briefs.deck: Indian boxer Gunjan has advanced to the women's 48kg final at the 2026 Summer Youth Olympics. She defeated Great Britain's Lily Bassett in the semifinals to secure her spot in the final. Gunjan will compete against Algeria's Bouthaina Bensalah for a chance to win gold. Earlier, Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei reached the final in the men's 50kg category.
briefs.bodyText:
Indian boxer Gunjan entered the women's 48kg final at the 2026 Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar, Senegal, on Wednesday, keeping India's hopes of winning a gold medal alive.
Gunjan defeated Great Britain's Lily Bassett 4-1 in the semifinal to book her place in the title clash. She became the second Indian boxer to reach the final in the competition.
The five judges scored the bout 30-27, 29-28, 28-29, 29-28 and 30-27, with four of them favouring the Indian boxer.
Gunjan will now face Algeria's Bouthaina Bensalah in the final. Bensalah booked her place in the title clash after beating Italy's Michela Guglielmon 3-2 in a close semifinal.
Gunjan assures India of a medal
Gunjan had started her campaign with a bye in the first round and moved straight into the quarterfinals. She then defeated Mexico's Atena Sofia Juarez Calero 5-0 to reach the semifinals and assure India of a medal.
Her semifinal victory has now given her a chance to turn that medal into gold.
Meetei also enters final
Earlier, Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei became the first Indian boxer to reach the final of the boxing competition at the 2026 Summer Youth Olympics.
Meetei defeated Colombia's Izzon Jeffrey Galea Arevalo 5-0 in the men's 50kg semifinal on Wednesday. Fighting from the red corner, the Indian boxer dominated the bout and received the backing of all five judges.
The judges scored the bout 28-27, 28-27, 28-27, 29-26 and 28-27.
Meetei will face Ireland's Kristian Jubani in the final. Jubani reached the title clash after beating Mexico's Alan Jesus Ocampo Cano 5-0 in the other semifinal.

briefs.headline: 'I'd tape it to my thumb': Ex-Australia star admits to using sandpaper
briefs.deck: Stuart MacGill has acknowledged using sandpaper on the ball during his cricket career, indicating it was not a deliberate cheating strategy. His admission follows recent statements made by Usman Khawaja in his memoir, which has reopened discussions on Sandpapergate. Cricket Australia maintains that the wider team was unaware of any wrongdoing during the 2018 Cape Town Test.
briefs.bodyText:
The Sandpapergate controversy has resurfaced in Australian cricket, eight years after the 2018 scandal. Following fresh revelations by former Australia batter 
Usman Khawaja
 in his memoir, 'Sabr', ex-leg-spinner 
Stuart MacGill
 has now admitted to using sandpaper on the ball during his playing career.
MacGill, who played 44 Tests and three ODIs for Australia between 1998 and 2008, said he had used sandpaper on the ball but insisted that it was not part of a bigger plan to cheat.
His admission has added another twist to the Sandpapergate controversy, which took place during Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018. The incident had led to bans for three Australian players and remains one of the biggest controversies in Australian cricket.
MacGill reveals how he used sandpaper
Speaking to former Sydney Sixers teammates Steve O'Keefe and Moises Henriques on a FanaticsTV YouTube show, MacGill explained how he would attach a small piece of sandpaper to his thumb and use it to scratch the ball.
"I'd cut a small piece of sandpaper and tape it to my thumb," he said. "It was not a part of a massive 'global cheating scam'; I was just really curious to see what would happen and if it would work. And oh, it works (laughs)," said MacGill.
He also explained how he would use the sandpaper after tea, remove it from his thumb and throw it away before the match continued.
"What they would do is the umpires as you're walking out on the ground, they used to put the ball sort of about 20 metres over the boundary and leave it there and you'd run out on the field, pick it up and go on the field. I would tape a little bit of a square of sandpaper on my thumb, pick the ball up just after tea, scratch the living daylights out of it, pull the sandpaper off, chuck it in the gutter before a ball had even been bowled. So nobody even knew that I'd done it, apart from all the scratches on the ball," he added.
Khawaja's claims reopen Sandpapergate
MacGill's admission comes after Khawaja made fresh claims about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in his memoir, 'Sabr'.
Cricket Australia has maintained that the wider Australian team was not aware of the plan to use sandpaper to change the condition of the ball during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.
However, Khawaja's revelations have raised fresh questions about what other players knew about the incident.
Darren Lehmann, who was Australia's head coach during the 2018 tour of South Africa, has strongly denied knowing about the plan to use sandpaper. Players such as Mitchell Starc have also publicly denied any involvement in the scandal.
Former Australia captain David Warner, one of the three players punished over the incident, has backed Khawaja and said that the claims in his autobiography are true.

briefs.headline: 'Pace is good, but skills matter': Auqib Nabi on adapting to New Zealand conditions
briefs.deck: Auqib Nabi had a quiet start to the five-match series, returning figures of 0/33 in the first ODI, which India won by five wickets (DLS method). He bounced back in the second match, dismissing New Zealand openers Will Young and Tim Seifert to help India register a four-run victory (DLS method). The third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned due to rain, with India leading the series 2-0.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India pacer Auqib Nabi believes that having pace is an advantage, but trusting one's skills is equally important. The Jammu and Kashmir pacer says he will stick to the methods that brought him success in domestic cricket as he prepares for the fourth ODI against New Zealand.
Nabi had a quiet start to the five-match series, returning figures of 0/33 in the first ODI, which India won by five wickets (DLS method).
He bounced back in the second match, dismissing New Zealand openers Will Young and Tim Seifert to help India register a four-run victory (DLS method).
The third ODI in Hamilton was abandoned due to rain, with India leading the series 2-0. The fourth match will be played at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on Friday.
"Having pace is good but I back my skills. I will do what I have been doing and what has brought me here. I will just do what I did in domestic cricket, and that will help me here too," Nabi said during the press conference ahead of the fourth ODI.
Learning to bowl in New Zealand conditions
Playing his first series in New Zealand, Nabi knows that he will need to adapt to the conditions. The pacer believes that seam movement will be important, as batters can deal with swing bowling.
"It is my first time in New Zealand. You need to rely more on seam here. Use scrambled seam because swing can be dealt with," he said.
Nabi also highlighted the importance of bowling with discipline, particularly on good batting pitches where bowlers can easily leak runs.
"You need to bowl well no matter how good or flat the pitches are. When wickets are good, you need to bowl with discipline because you can go for runs," he said.
"We keep discussing amongst ourselves about plans for drop-in pitches. With Arshdeep and Anshul both," he said.
"Weather back home and here is similar. Opposition and level of cricket is different," he said.
From Ranji Trophy success to India colours
Known as the 'Baramulla Express', Nabi earned his place in the Indian team through consistent performances in domestic cricket.
The Jammu and Kashmir pacer picked up 104 wickets across the 2024-25 and 2025-26 Ranji Trophy seasons. His standout performance came in the 2025-26 season, when he picked 60 wickets in 17 innings at an average of 12.65. His efforts played a key role in Jammu and Kashmir winning their maiden Ranji Trophy title. He was also named Player of the Tournament.
Nabi admitted that he had expected a Test call-up before getting an opportunity in white-ball cricket. However, he believes the current experience will help him when he gets another chance in the red-ball format.
"I was expecting a red-ball call-up before white-ball cricket, but this experience will also be very helpful. And then also staying with the Test team," he said.
"Very happy to play for India. Khelna India ke liye bahut badi baat hai. Mera bhi wohi tha," he added.
"Whenever people say about facilities, I always say do your best and things will fall in place," the pacer said.

briefs.headline: Ambekar Meetei storms into men’s 50kg final at Youth Olympics
briefs.deck: Ambekar’s semifinal victory against the Colombian ended a 16-year wait for an Indian boxer in a Youth Olympics final, matching the milestone set by Shiva Thapa at the inaugural Singapore 2010 Games
briefs.bodyText:
India's Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei stormed into the men's 50kg boxing final at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games after registering a commanding 5-0 victory over Colombia's Izzon Jeffrey Galea Arevalo in the semifinals.
Ambekar Meetei dominated the contest to secure a unanimous points verdict and book his place in the gold medal bout.
He will now look to cap his campaign with a gold medal.
Ambekar's semifinal victory against the Colombian ended a 16-year wait for an Indian boxer in a Youth Olympics final, matching the milestone set by Shiva Thapa at the inaugural Singapore 2010 Games.
From Manipur, Ambekar trains at the National Institute of Sports (NIS) in Patiala.
